# What the evidence establishes {.unnumbered}

Across the four checks the package behaves as its design promises. On the
fixed-effects problem with a known answer, the INLA back end reproduces the
ordinary-least-squares solution to a precision far below the estimation
uncertainty, so the translation to a Gaussian linear model is exact. On the
`sleepstudy` random-intercept model, `flexyBayes` through INLA reproduces a
hand-written `INLA::inla()` fit to numerical precision, which shows the package
builds the model the user specified rather than a near neighbour, and it lands
within the reference fit's standard error of the `lme4` REML estimate. The two
sampling back ends, greta through Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and `brms` through
Stan, both agree with the same reference on the slope and intercept within
sampling tolerance.

Two qualifications travel with the evidence, both stated where they
arise. The greta fit at a modest warm-up carried convergence warnings from the
package itself, so a publication fit should lengthen the warm-up even though the
agreement test still passes. And the `brms` comparison matched only the slope
term by name across all three fits, because the intercept carries a different
canonical label in each, a naming question rather than a numerical disagreement.

Taken together, one model specification fitted three ways gives concordant
estimates, and the cross-back-end agreement is the triangulation signal the
package is built to provide.
